texto_en: Autism and mental health: coexistence, not equivalence
A 2019 meta-analysis that included 96 studies in its analyses calculated the following pooled prevalences among autistic people:
studies included in a meta-analysis published in 2019 · Lai et al., 2019.

The percentages represent pooled prevalences of coexisting conditions within samples of autistic people. They are useful for showing that care cannot be reduced to a single label, but they do not predict what will happen for any one person.
Present the percentages as pooled prevalences of coexisting conditions in a meta-analysis. They are not individual probabilities and heterogeneity was very high.

Unexplained heterogeneity was very high —I² above 95%— and figures changed according to age, sex, intellectual functioning, country and type of sample. Clinical studies produced higher prevalences than population-based or registry studies.
More than 1.3 billion people —around 16% of the world population, 1 in 6— live with a significant disability.
current global estimate · WHO Europe, update 10-08-2026.
WHO keeps this estimate in its European update of 10 August 2026.

WHO uses a broad category of significant disability. It is contextual data for studying barriers in health, education, employment and participation; it is not an estimate of the neurodivergent population.
Cite 1.3 billion, 16% and 1 in 6 as three ways of expressing the same estimate. Do not use ‘disability’ as a synonym for ‘neurodivergence’.

Disability is not a synonym for neurodivergence. This figure is used to describe barriers in health, education, employment, mobility and participation affecting the disabled population, within which part of the neurodivergent population is included.

Health differences associated with disability are not explained only by underlying conditions. WHO identifies health-service barriers, inaccessible transport, poverty, stigma and exclusion from education and employment as factors that produce avoidable inequality.
